Posted January 3, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan Sponsored by Advanced Nutrients

There are several challenges being mounted to the Canadian cannabis laws that may well result in their being overturned in the BC courts. Below is a press release from Michele Kubby, complaining that she has been unable even to get on the role to have her case heard.

Her immediate objective is to get a Constitutional exemption that would allow her to legally use medical cannabis. A variety of Canadian courts have repeatedly ruled that sick and dying Canadians have a right to use the plant. While the US Supreme Court will rule later this year on whether Americans have such a right, it is settled law in Canada.
See
 We Have Already Won A Lot From The Supreme Court Case, Which Is Good Because That Is Probably All That We Are Going To Get. DEA Changes The Rules on Treating Pain.

For Immediate Release
January 4, 2005

Today, Michele Kubby, wife of cancer patient and medical cannabis refugee Steve Kubby, wrote to the Chief Justice Supreme Court of British Columbia, D. I. Brenner, in pursuit of a hearing on her right to be granted a Constitutional exemption that would allow her to use medical cannabis.

Mrs. Kubby, whose use of medical cannabis has been recommended by a number of doctors, including a leading specialist, complained, It appears to be an impossible task to have this matter placed on the Role and heard by this Honourable Court, notwithstanding the five months that have passed since this matter was filed.

However, she is not only seeking a personal exemption. She is also seeking to have the BC courts rule that the laws against marihuana violate Charter 7 rights and are without force and effect and are null and void. If she prevails in her argument, it would have the effect of voiding the laws against cannabis in Canada.

She wrote to the Chief Justice, I am being denied my right to access marihuana solely because the criminal justice system, [the Courts] have usurped Charter s. 33 (1) and refuse to comply with the Constitution Act 1982 s. 52 (1), choosing instead to write and follow purported and pretended judicial enactments and the obiter dicta of judgments such as the Ontario Court of Appeal in Hitzig et al (2003) rather than the Constitution.

CONTACT:
Michele Kubby, 250-578-8422

There are several reasons to think that the cannabis laws, perhaps in their entirety, but at least as they pertain to personal use and cultivation, as well as cultivating and supplying cannabis to patients, are in fact, without force and effect and are null and void as a result of Health Canada's repeated failure to obey various Court rulings.

A little history.

In July of 2000, after a long battle, the Ontario Court of Appeals ruled in the Terry Parker case that the failure to provide for a realistic way for sick and dying Canadians to get medical access to cannabis voided the laws against possession.
See
 Canadian Court Says Lack of Provision for Medical Marijuana Violates Fundamental Rights; Gives Parliament 12 Months to Fix Marijuana Prohibition
-- Or There Will Be No Marijuana Laws in Canada.

The ruling said, Accordingly, I would declare the prohibition on the possession of marihuana in the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act to be of no force and effect. However, since this would leave a gap in the regulatory scheme until Parliament could amend the legislation to comply with the Charter, I would suspend the declaration of invalidity for a year. During this period, the marihuana law remains in full force and effect. Parker, however, cannot be deprived of his rights during this year and therefore he is entitled to a personal exemption from the possession offence under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act for possessing marihuana for his medical needs.

In other words, the judge was holding the law against non-medical use hostage for one year in order to force the Parliament not Health Canada to make a new law. For whatever reason, HC did not appeal the court's ruling, so it became binding on the Canadian government.
See
 Canada Will Not Appeal Court Ruling Requiring Medical Marijuana.
and links

Nonetheless, for nine months they did nothing, then on April 6, 2001, they submitted new rules that actually made the problem worse in many ways.
See
 We Are Winning! Canadian Medical Marijuana Program: Politically Very Important, Medically and Scientifically Absurd.

Ultimately, this charade did not satisfy the courts. As the Ontario Court said in its Hitzig ruling: In R. v. Parker, supra, this court declared the prohibition invalid as of July 31, 2001 if by that date the Government had not enacted a constitutionally sound medical exemption. Our decision in this case confirms that it did not do so. Hence the marihuana prohibition in s. 4 has been of no force or effect since July 31, 2001.

However, in its Hitzig ruling, the Ontario Court required certain changes in the Government's medical cannabis program, and then held, our order has the result of constitutionalizing the medical exemption created by the Government. As a result, the marihuana prohibition in s. 4 is no longer inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution.

Although Parliament may subsequently choose to change it, that prohibition is now no longer invalid, but is of full force and effect. Those who establish medical need are simply exempted from it.

Our remedy quite precisely determines the barriers in the MMAR which, if removed, would render it a constitutionally sound medical exemption (emphasis added) to s. 4 of the CDSA. Our order represents a minimal intrusion on the Government's scheme of medical exemption. It leaves untouched the licensed possession aspect of the scheme and modifies the licensed production aspect of itonly enough to make it constitutionally acceptable. (emphasis added)

In other words, the Court did the least it could in order to make cannabis prohibition constitutional, but

First, it is not at all clear that the Court actually reinstated the laws, or whether it simply gave an order, which IF IMPLEMENTED would have made prohibition constitutional.

Second, it should be noted that there is a serious question as to whether a court could actually revive a law after it had been of no force or effect since July 31, 2001. After all, the Court said that Parliament could amend the legislation to comply with the Charter. It is not the job of the courts to rewrite bad laws.

However, as we shall see, these may be moot points.

The sad fact is that Health Canada has consistently thumbed its bureaucratic nose at the courts, and in Canada, the courts have an odd way of letting the government do that up to a point. Thus a challenge in the relatively friendly venue of the BC Courts would make very clear that HC never obeyed even the Ontario Court's minimal intrusion on the Government's scheme of medical exemption...

Therefore, if that is the case, then it should be quite clear that the Ontario Court ruling did not reinstate cannabis prohibition, because HC never met their minimum requirements. These are the arguments in Michele Kubby's petition to the BC Supreme Court.

I am enormously grateful to Philippe Lucas of the Vancouver Island Compassion Society and Canadians for Safe Access for his detailed analysis of Health Canada's refusal to obey the law. Philippe is one of the most effective activists in the medical cannabis movement.
See
 Hypocrisy and Democracy: Raid on Medical Cannabis Research Facility Critical of Health Canada's Schwag Challenges Canada's Values. What Will The Politicians Say?
and
 Canadian Medical Cannabis Patients Denounce Health Canada's War On Sick And Dying As New Survey Shows MARIJUANA LAWS A TOTAL FAILURE

I have posted Philippe's analysis on a separate webpage to make it easier to access.
See
 Philippe Lucas Analysis of the Consequences of Health Canada's Failure to Obey the Ontario Court's Ruling On Medical Cannabis. Is Cannabis Legal in Canada?
